name: Aisha Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a business degree with an accounting route, which my dad insisted on. He and my uncle run a tile shop, so I grew up doing stock counts on Sundays. I live in a shared flat with two girls from my course and I go home to my parents most weekends to help in the shop and do my laundry. I don't use AI for anything. My lecturers keep suggesting it, but I'd rather do the work myself and know I understand it. The first term has been a lot of new faces, and I'm not great at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it. Some things get a bit quicker, fine. I'd tell my family the shop's accounts still need a person who understands them, and I'd stay quiet online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, relief. Accounting's one of those jobs people say could be automated, and a plateau means my dad's plan holds. But I know firms already use software for the dull parts, and I don't want to be the dull part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as now. I'd keep the weekend shifts at the shop, study hard to get a good first-year mark, and aim for a placement year at a mid-sized accounting firm. I'd keep my spending down. My parents give me three hundred a month and I'm not going to ask for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. Not about AI, but about whether I'll be good enough. I'm worried about exams and about whether I'll find the placement, because I find it hard to meet strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use it because I don't understand how it works, and I don't want to depend on something I can't check. My cousin used it for an essay and it made up a source. That put me off for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you to feel secure about accounting as a career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly knowing a firm wants me, with a placement and then a job. After that, savings. My parents never took a holiday for ten years because of the shop. I'd like to have an income that doesn't depend on whether tiles sell.

say: I'd say **good**, I never trusted it, and the shop's accounts still need a person.
think: I'm relieved, because accounting is called **automatable** and a plateau keeps my dad's plan alive.
Firms already automate the dull parts, and I don't want to be them.
do: Keep my **weekend shifts** at the tile shop.
Aim for a good first-year mark and a **placement year** at an accounting firm.
Keep spending within the **three hundred pounds** my parents send.
feel: **Uneasy**, but about being good enough and meeting strangers, not about AI itself.
S0.quote: I don't want to depend on something I can't check.
fieldNote: Resistance to AI is built on a **specific experience**, her cousin's fake citation.
Her anxiety is social and about performance, not technological.
Family pressure and the shop's history sit behind her cautious choices.

steps.text: Work weekend shifts at the family tile shop
Aim for a first-year mark good enough for placements
Keep spending within the three hundred monthly allowance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. Every few years something is going to change everything. I'd tell my friends to do the degree anyway and keep options open. Online I'd read what others say but not post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried. Checking and bookkeeping are the first things to go. If the junior jobs at firms shrink, I might finish the degree and not get a placement. I think about that on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to move towards the parts of accounting that need judgement, like tax advice and talking to clients. I'd ask the careers service about firms that still hire juniors. I'd also ask my dad to teach me more of the shop's finances, and save a bit more. But I'd still avoid using AI, if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A slow change is almost worse, because you don't know when it will land on you. I'd rather have a clear date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Accounting is checking and planning work, which is on the card. What do you make of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't really blame anyone. Companies do what saves money, it's the way it works. I'd just say the government should help people retrain, but not much more than that. I don't like making a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the accounting jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My worry is that my not using AI becomes a problem. If everyone else is quick with it and I'm not, I'd stand out in a bad way. So maybe I'd have to try it once a week, just to understand it. I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

say: I'd say **we'll see**, since every few years something is meant to change everything.
Online I'd read what others post and say nothing.
think: Checking and bookkeeping go first, so I might finish and **not get a placement**.
I think about that on the **bus**.
do: Move towards **tax advice** and client work that needs judgement.
Ask the careers service which firms still hire **juniors**.
Ask Dad to teach me the shop's **finances**.
feel: **Anxious**, and a slow change is almost worse because the date is unclear.
S1.quote: A slow change is almost worse, because you don't know when it will land on you. I'd rather have a clear date.
fieldNote: Avoids blame; her style is **practical** acceptance, with a mild call for retraining help.
Notes that her avoidance of AI may become her own problem.
Concern is concrete: whether a placement exists.

steps.text: Ask the careers service which firms still hire junior accountants
Learn the shop's accounts properly from Dad
Choose tax and advisory modules over bookkeeping ones
Try an AI tool once a week to understand it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say very little in public. I'd say I'm waiting to see what the university says. Privately I'd be on the phone to my mum every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think the whole accounting plan is over. In 2028 I'd be at the end of second year, and by the time I graduate there'd be no junior accounting jobs. It would feel like Dad's plan for me has been cancelled. I might cry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the shop more, because tiles can't be laid by software for three more years at least. I'd ask my parents what we should do with the savings. I'd probably switch to a business degree without the accounting route, or ask about courses in trades, project management or construction. I'd cut my spending to a hundred a month and avoid debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Afraid, really. I like having a plan, and this takes the plan away. I'd probably get quiet and stop talking to my flatmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, would you stay on the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight, and he'd go quiet, then say we'll manage. He's practical. He'd say the shop's not going anywhere for a while and that I could run it with him. I never thought I'd want that, but I might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel telling your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots gap matters a lot to me. The shop is hands-on, so we'd have until 2031 at least, and I'd have time to learn the family trade. It's not what I planned, but it's something solid. That's why I'd go home more.

say: I'd say **very little** in public, only that I'm waiting to hear from the university.
I'd phone my mum every night.
think: The whole **accounting plan** would be over, and Dad's plan for me cancelled.
There would be **no junior jobs** by the time I graduate.
do: Spend more time at the **tile shop**, which robots reach later.
Ask about switching to **project management** or construction.
Cut spending to **a hundred pounds** a month and avoid more debt.
feel: **Alarmed** and afraid, because the plan I liked is gone.
S2.quote: The shop is hands-on, so we'd have until 2031 at least, and I'd have time to learn the family trade.
fieldNote: Withdrawal is her stress response: **quiet** with flatmates, busy with family.
The family shop becomes a lifeboat she did not plan on.
Sharp contrast with the first two scenarios, as her chosen field is directly hit.

steps.text: Spend weekdays off campus helping run the tile shop
Ask about switching to project management or construction
Cut spending to a hundred pounds a month
Talk with my parents about using the shop savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time to adjust, as long as people actually do. I'd say it quietly to my friends and not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I probably get a job and some experience, then lose it, and that's a bit cruel. But at least I'd have savings by then, and the tile shop to fall back on. That's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a decent mark and aim for a job at a small firm that does client work. I'd save about three hundred pounds a month from my first salary. I'd learn a little more about how the shop's money works. And I might ask my parents if I could take it over slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, going to anxious. There's time, but I'm not a person who changes fast. I'd need a plan written down, with dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, you'd graduate. How does that change the mood?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm a student with no plan. With five I'm a graduate with a job, so I'd have a bit of padding. But what really helps is that it's slow enough that I'd get used to it. I'm not good with shocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year after graduating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year after I graduate, I'd work, save and stay close to my family. I'd consider the shop properly then. I'd also probably give up and learn the AI tools, since everyone at work would be using them. I'd do it because I have to.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** to adjust, if people actually do.
I'd say it quietly to friends and not online.
think: I'd get a job and some experience, then **lose it**, which feels cruel.
At least I'd have **savings** and the tile shop to fall back on.
do: Finish the degree and aim for a **small firm** that does client work.
Save **three hundred pounds** a month from the first salary.
Ask my parents about **taking over** the shop slowly.
feel: Between uneasy and anxious, since I'm **not good** with shocks and need a written plan.
S3.quote: I'm not a person who changes fast. I'd need a plan written down, with dates.
fieldNote: Needs **structure** to feel safe, and the five-year gap gives her some.
Acknowledges she would eventually have to use AI tools, though reluctantly.
The family shop is a recurring safety net.

steps.text: Finish first-year accounting modules with a solid mark
Apply to small firms that do client accounts after graduating
Save three hundred pounds a month from first pay
Ask my parents about taking over the shop slowly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news, and I'd stop worrying so much. I'd tell my parents the shop could be passed on, and I'd say nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think it's very long. A lot can change and I might have a family by then. I could have ten years as an accountant before it matters. That's a whole career, almost. I'd still worry, but at a lower level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work as an accountant for several years, and save steadily. I'd probably retrain in something advisory or human-facing by year five. I'd keep up with the shop, maybe becoming a co-owner. I'd start learning the AI tools slowly, one at a time, starting in my final year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit anxious about my own habits, but the situation itself feels manageable. I like that I'd get to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot of time. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a proper accounting job, then work towards a role in a firm that deals with people. I'd save and consider buying a flat. If I do it right, I'd have money before the robots arrive for hands-on work. Ten years is long enough to be sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you, even with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about whether my parents' shop will survive until then, and whether I'd be good at changing. I'm slow to try new things. If I keep avoiding AI for ten years I'd be left behind, and I know that.

say: I'd say it's **good news** and I'd stop worrying so much.
I'd tell my parents the shop could be **passed on**.
think: Ten years is **a whole career**, almost, so I'd worry at a lower level.
I might even have a **family** by then.
do: Work as an **accountant** for several years and save steadily.
Retrain in something **advisory** or human-facing by year five.
Learn the AI tools slowly, one at a time, from my **final year**.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with some worry about my own habits.
S4.quote: If I keep avoiding AI for ten years I'd be left behind, and I know that.
fieldNote: Honest about her own **resistance**, naming it as the real risk.
Long horizon turns plans into steady, modest steps.
Family shop appears again as both worry and anchor.

steps.text: Work as a junior accountant and save steadily for years
Retrain in advisory or client-facing accounting by year five
Start learning one AI tool at a time in final year
Help my parents plan the shop's future

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, definitely. I'd be in the middle of a degree for a job that would be gone, and I wouldn't have time to think. What would help is somebody telling me clearly what to do, like a careers advisor with a real plan, and my parents being okay with me changing course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I don't think so. I talk too slowly for these things, but I'd say I'm not as afraid of AI as of being unprepared. I just want to know the plan, even if the plan is hard.

headlineQuote: I'm not as afraid of AI as of being unprepared. I just want to know the plan, even if the plan is hard.
portrait: **Aisha Silva** is 18, a business student on an accounting route, helping in her family's tile shop on weekends.
She **never uses AI** and distrusts it after her cousin's essay invented a source.
She is cautious and shy, avoids fuss, and blames no one in particular.
Her mood moves from uneasy to **alarmed** if AGI comes in two years, then eases with more time.
The family shop is her fallback, and she wants a clear plan with dates.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries her most, with a degree for a job that would be gone.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a careers advisor with a **real plan** and her parents' support if she changes course.
